theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A large gate is built from three sub-assemblies: two leaves and a frame. Why is it often best to build and check each sub-assembly first?
options: Faults are easier to find and fix on smaller parts
Sub-assemblies need no drawing or measuring at all
It means the welds will not need to be inspected
It uses more clamps, which keeps the parts cooler

questions.stem: What is a bill of materials (parts list) on an assembly drawing used for?
options: To show the order in which the welds are made
To show the price the customer will pay
To list every part, its size, material and number
To list the people who will work on the job

questions.stem: Why should parts coming from the cutting and forming bays be checked before assembly starts?
options: So the assembly bay can stay busy all day
A wrong part found now saves rework later
So the parts can be painted before fitting
So that no tolerance is needed on the drawing

questions.stem: A steel water tank stand for a house in Spanish Town will be bolted together on site. What should the leader check before the parts leave the workshop?
options: That the paint colour matches the house
That the parts are as heavy as possible
That every part is welded together into one piece
All parts, fixings and tools against the parts list

questions.stem: Why should the order of assembly be planned to leave room for welding every joint?
options: So the welder can work faster and skip all the tacks
So the assembly can be lifted with one hand
Some joints cannot be reached once others are fitted
So the drawing does not need weld symbols

questions.stem: On an assembly drawing, a weld symbol has a small flag where the arrow line bends. What does the flag mean?
options: Make this weld on site, not in the workshop
Grind this weld flush and smooth after welding
Use a fillet weld at this joint
This weld must be tested by X-ray

questions.stem: A roof truss has a base of 2 400 mm and a height of 500 mm at the centre. Using Pythagoras, how long is each sloping member, centre to corner?
Two strings are stretched across the diagonals of a frame lying on a flat table. They just touch where they cross. What does this show?
options: The frame is square, but may still be twisted
The frame is flat, with no twist (wind)
The frame is the right length and width
The frame's welds are strong enough

questions.stem: Why should a steel tape be checked against a known length before it is used to set out a large job?
options: A worn or bent hook can make every reading wrong
Tapes always read short until they are warmed up
Tapes lose their numbers if they are not checked
So it can be used as a straight edge too

questions.stem: Why is a large frame often set out full size on the table, with chalk lines and stops, before any parts are placed?
options: So that the parts do not need to be cut to any size
So the frame can be built without any clamps
Each part can be placed to the lines and checked
So the welder knows what colour to paint it

questions.stem: Four parts are fitted end to end. Each is allowed ±0.5 mm. What is the worst possible error in the total length?
A long frame is measured in the hot afternoon sun and again in the cool of the morning. Why might the two readings differ slightly?
options: The tape reads differently in the morning light
The welds keep shrinking for many weeks
Frames always shrink overnight as they settle
Steel grows a little as it warms up

questions.stem: Why should a jig locate each part against fixed stops, and not just clamp it anywhere?
options: So every part sits in the same place each time
So that the clamps can be made of plastic
So the parts can move about freely while they are welded
So that no drawing is needed for the job

questions.stem: A part is clamped hard against a jig and then welded. What can happen when the clamps are released?
options: Nothing; the clamps take away all stresses
The part grows larger than it was
It may spring a little out of line
The welds will fall apart at once

questions.stem: What is a strongback used for in plate assembly?
options: Lifting the heavy frames off the table
Bending plate into a curve
Measuring the gap at the root
Holding plate edges level for welding

questions.stem: Why are magnetic squares moved away before a weld close to them is made?
options: Magnets make the weld metal turn hard
Magnets can pull the arc off line (arc blow)
Magnets stop the steel parts from getting hot at all
Magnets melt at welding temperature

questions.stem: A fit-up check is made before full welding. Which of these is checked at this stage?
options: The thickness of the final coat of paint
The weld throat size
Root gaps, alignment and tack quality
The customer's payment

questions.stem: Two plates in a butt joint are not level: one edge sits 3 mm higher than the other (mismatch). What should be done before welding?
options: Bring the edges level with a strongback or clamp
Weld it as it is and grind the high side later
Fill the step with extra weld metal
Leave it, as some mismatch makes the joint stronger

questions.stem: Why must tack welds be made with the same care, and to the same procedure, as the final weld?
options: Tacks are always ground out before welding
Tacks become part of the final weld
So the tacks can be made with any electrode
So the tacks are as large as possible

questions.stem: Why are the ends of tack welds often ground to a taper on joints that will be welded over?
options: So the tacks can be seen easily by the inspector
So the tacks are weaker and break off later
So that less filler is needed in the root
So the final weld fuses smoothly into them

questions.stem: On a fitted joint, the root gap is too wide in one place. What is the best course?
options: Re-fit the parts to the right gap before welding
Bridge it with a piece of filler rod laid in the gap
Weld it anyway with a bigger electrode
Fill the gap with many fast passes

questions.stem: A tee joint is to be welded on one side only. Why might the upright be set leaning slightly away from the weld side first (pre-set)?
options: So the weld will be easier to reach and see
So that less weld metal is needed
Weld shrinkage pulls it back to square
So the joint does not need any tacks

questions.stem: Which is the best way to reduce distortion when welding a long beam made from plates?
options: Weld one side fully, then turn it and weld the other
Use the largest electrode and the slowest travel
Leave out the tacks so that the plates can move
Weld in short runs, balanced on both sides

questions.stem: Why should a welded assembly not be taken out of its jig while it is still hot?
options: Hot steel is too heavy to lift safely
It can move as it cools if it is not held
The jig will rust if parts are left in it
Hot parts weigh less than cold parts

questions.stem: Where the drawing allows it, why is intermittent (stitch) welding sometimes used instead of a continuous weld?
options: Less heat goes in, so there is less distortion
It is always stronger than a continuous weld
It needs no fit-up checks before welding
It stops water getting into the joint

questions.stem: What does '8.8' marked on the head of a metric bolt tell you?
options: The bolt is 8.8 mm in diameter
The bolt is 88 mm long
The thread pitch is 8.8 threads in each inch
The bolt's strength grade (property class)

questions.stem: Why should the nut used on a high-strength bolt be of the matching grade?
options: So that the colours of the bolt and nut match
A weaker nut is easier to tighten fully
A weak nut can strip before the bolt is tight
So the nut can be used without a washer

questions.stem: Why do torque figures for bolts depend on whether the threads are oiled or dry?
options: Oil makes the bolt stronger, so it needs less torque
Oil cuts friction, so the bolt is pulled tighter
Oil stops the torque wrench from clicking
Dry threads cannot be tightened at all

questions.stem: Why are slotted holes sometimes used in a bracket that will be bolted in place on site?
options: To allow a little adjustment to line it up
To make the bracket stronger in every direction
So the bolts do not need to be tightened
So no washers are ever needed

questions.stem: Two pieces of 1.5 mm sheet are to be joined with blind rivets. How is the right rivet length chosen?
options: As long as possible, so it holds better
Always the same as the hole diameter
Half the total thickness of the sheets
From the maker's grip range for 3 mm

questions.stem: Aluminium sheet is to be riveted. Why should aluminium rivets be used rather than steel ones?
options: Steel rivets are too weak to hold aluminium
Aluminium rivets are easier to see once fitted
Mixed metals can corrode when they get wet
Steel rivets cannot be set by a rivet gun

questions.stem: Rivets in a lap joint must not be placed too close to the edge of the sheet. Why?
options: The rivet gun cannot reach near the edge
The sheet can tear out between rivet and edge
The rivet will be far too loose to set properly
The edge will rust faster than the middle

questions.stem: Holding-down bolts are set into a new concrete base for a tank stand. When can the stand be bolted down and loaded?
options: When it has cured for the time the maker gives
At once, as soon as the bolts are in place
After one hour, whatever the weather
As soon as the top of the concrete looks dry

questions.stem: An assembled frame weighs about 180 kg. How should it be moved off the table?
options: By four trainees lifting it quickly together
By one strong person, using the legs
By sliding it off the edge onto the floor
With a crane, hoist or trolley, under a plan

questions.stem: A heavy part is being lowered by a hoist into position for fitting. Where should the fitters' hands be?
options: Under the load, ready to guide it into place
Clear of pinch points, never under the load
Holding the hoist chain to keep it still
On the hook, so the load cannot swing

questions.stem: When tacks on an assembly are ground, why must the grinder's guard stay on and the disc be rated for the grinder's speed?
options: So that the disc wears more slowly
So the sparks are a nicer colour
A burst disc can cause serious injury
So the grinder can be used without gloves

questions.stem: A fitter needs to work under a large frame that is raised up off the table. What must be done first?
options: Support it securely on stands so it cannot fall
Ask a trainee to hold it up by hand
Prop it on a pile of offcuts
Work very quickly so that the time at risk is short

questions.stem: What is a 'hold point' in an inspection plan?
options: The place where finished work is stored
A clamp that holds parts while they are welded
The point where a lifting sling is attached
A stage where work stops until it is inspected

questions.stem: An assembled frame is 4 mm outside the tolerance, but the customer may still accept it. What is the correct way to handle this?
options: Send it out and hope the customer does not notice
Change the drawing yourself to match the frame
Record it and get written approval before sending it
Scrap it at once without telling anyone

questions.stem: Why are the actual measurements written on an inspection record, and not just a tick?
options: So the record looks longer and more complete
They show how close it is and reveal trends
So the inspector can be paid by the hour
Ticks are not allowed on any form

questions.stem: Why are two mating parts often clamped together and drilled as a pair?
options: So the holes in both parts line up exactly
So the drill bit lasts twice as long
So that no centre punch mark is ever needed
So the parts can be painted together

questions.stem: A frame passes all its dimensional checks. Which other check is still needed before it is passed?
options: The weight of the frame on a bathroom scale
Whether the trainees enjoyed the job
The colour of the steel before painting
Visual checks of welds, fixings and finish

questions.stem: You lead a team of four. One member's tacks are often too small and crack. What is the best action?
options: Do all the tacks yourself from now on
Tell the others to avoid working with him
Watch him, find the cause and coach him
Report him for poor work and say nothing

questions.stem: At the start of an assembly job, what should the team leader's briefing cover?
options: Only the time the job must be finished
The drawing, tasks, hazards and quality checks
The leader's own pay and hours of work
The names of last year's best trainees

questions.stem: When an assembly is handed over, which document helps the customer and the Centre most if a question comes up later?
options: A signed record of the checks and results
A photo of the team at lunch
The receipt for the welding electrodes used
The workshop's cleaning roster

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the steel section with a hollow square or rectangular cross-section, often used for gates and frames?
A frame has 4 brackets, each fixed with 4 bolts. Every bolt has 2 washers and 1 nut. How many washers are needed?
On a weld symbol, what does a small circle drawn where the arrow line bends mean?
What is the name of the document raised when work does not meet the drawing or specification?
In metric units, what unit is bolt tightening torque measured in?
What is the name of the liquid put on bolt threads that sets and stops the nut working loose?
A gate frame is 1 800 mm wide and the opening between the posts is 1 830 mm. What is the total clearance left for the hinges and latch, in mm?
A frame is made from two lengths of tube of 1 200 mm and two of 800 mm. What total length of tube is needed, in metres?
What is the name for the point, line or edge from which all the measurements on a drawing or part are taken?
What is the name for dipping steel in molten zinc to protect gates and grills from rust in salty sea air?
What is the name of the steel plate welded to the bottom of a column or leg, with holes for the holding-down bolts?
What is the name of the triangular plate welded into a corner of a frame to stiffen it?
What is the name for a slight upward curve built into a beam on purpose, so that it is straight when it is loaded?
What tool projects a level beam of light across a site so that heights can be set and checked?
What do the letters NDT stand for, when welds and parts are tested without damaging them?

essays.stem: You are in charge of building a steel water tank stand (four legs, bracing and a top frame) for a house in St Catherine. Explain how you would plan the assembly: the sub-assemblies, the sequence, the jigs, the people and the inspection points.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing and parts list for the sizes, materials, welds and fixings, and check every part against the list. I split the stand into sub-assemblies: two side frames, each with two legs and their bracing, and the top frame. Each sub-assembly is built flat on the setting-out table, to lines and stops, so that it can be checked for square, size and twist before it is joined. I plan the order so that every weld can be reached: weld the side frames, then join them with the cross-bracing and the top frame, checking plumb and diagonals as we go. I set hold points: after the fit-up of each sub-assembly, after welding, and on the final assembly, including the base plate hole positions so the holding-down bolts will fit. I give each member a task: marking out, fitting, tacking and welding, checking, and operating the hoist. I plan the lifting, because the side frames are heavy, and I record each check on the inspection sheet.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and checks the parts against the list
Divides the job into sub-assemblies, built flat to lines and stops and checked
Plans a sequence that leaves every weld reachable, checking plumb and diagonals
Sets hold points, including the base plate hole positions
Gives tasks, plans the lifting and records the checks

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up a simple jig for making 20 identical gate frames, and how it helps both quality and speed.
essays.modelAnswer: A jig holds each part in exactly the same place every time, so all 20 frames are the same and fit their openings. I would build it on a flat, level setting-out table. First I mark the frame's outline full size from the drawing, starting from a datum corner, then fix stops (blocks or angle pieces) against the outside of each member at the corners and at the centre rail. The stops locate the parts on fixed points so that a part can only go in one way. I add quick-acting clamps to hold each part against its stops, placed where they do not get in the way of the welds, and leave a gap at each joint so it can be welded. I allow for shrinkage, for example by setting the stops a little over size if a test frame comes out small. I prove the jig with the first frame, checking the size, diagonals and flatness, and adjust it if needed. The jig speeds up the work because no marking out is needed for each frame, and quality improves because every frame is the same. I check the jig at intervals, as stops can move.
markingPoints: Purpose: every part in the same place, so every frame is the same
Built on a flat table from a full-size layout and a datum
Fixed stops to locate; clamps placed clear of the welds, with weld access
Allows for shrinkage and proves the jig on the first frame
Explains the gains in speed and quality, and checks the jig at intervals

essays.stem: Explain why welded assemblies distort, and describe four methods a fabricator uses to control distortion.
essays.modelAnswer: Distortion happens because weld metal and the hot steel around it expand when heated and then shrink as they cool. The cold metal around the weld holds it back, so the shrinking pulls the parts out of shape: angles close up, plates bow and frames twist. Four ways to control it: (1) Good fit-up and no more weld than needed: the right gaps, no oversize welds, and stitch welds where the drawing allows, so less heat goes in. (2) Balanced welding: a sequence that balances the shrinkage, such as opposite sides in turn, with back-step or skip welding on long joints. (3) Restraint: clamping the work in a jig or tacking on strongbacks so it cannot move while it is welded, and letting it cool before release. (4) Pre-setting: setting parts at a small angle the opposite way, so the shrinkage pulls them into line. Other methods are using enough tacks, welding from the centre outwards, and correcting small distortion afterwards by flame straightening.
markingPoints: Cause: expansion and shrinkage held back by cold metal
Less heat: good fit-up, right weld size, stitch welds where allowed
Balanced sequence, back-step or skip welding
Restraint with jigs, clamps or strongbacks, cooled before release
Pre-setting against the expected shrinkage

essays.stem: Describe a fit-up inspection made before welding: what you check, the tools you use, and what you do if the fit-up is not right.
essays.modelAnswer: A fit-up inspection is made after the parts are tacked and before full welding, because faults are cheap to fix now and costly later. I check that the parts are the right ones, in the right place and the right way round, against the drawing. I measure the main sizes with a tape, check squareness by the diagonals and with a square, and check flatness or twist with a straight edge or diagonal strings. At each joint I check the root gap and root face with a gauge, the bevel angle, and that the edges are level with no mismatch. I check that the joint faces are clean of rust, paint, oil and slag, that the tacks are sound and the right size with no cracks, and that the welder can reach every joint. If anything is wrong, the assembly is not welded: the tacks are ground out and the parts are fitted again, then checked again. I record the result and sign the hold point before welding begins.
markingPoints: Explains why fit-up is checked before welding
Checks parts, positions, main sizes, square and flatness with tape, square and strings
Checks root gap, root face, bevel and mismatch with gauges
Checks cleanliness, tack quality and weld access
If wrong: refit and recheck; records and signs the hold point

essays.stem: Explain how the bolt grade, hole size, washers, tightening order and torque affect a structural bolted joint, and how you would check the finished joint.
essays.modelAnswer: The bolt grade, such as 8.8, shows its strength, and the drawing states which grade to use; the nut must be of the matching grade, or its thread may strip. Holes are drilled to the size the drawing gives, usually a little larger than the bolt so it can be fitted without forcing; holes that are too big let the joint slip. Parts drilled together line up best. Washers spread the load under the nut and the bolt head and protect the surface; hardened washers are used where the specification asks for them. The bolts are first snugged up, then tightened in a criss-cross order from the centre out, so that the parts pull together evenly. The final tightening is done with a torque wrench to the figure the specification or maker gives, remembering that oiled or dry threads change the tension a torque gives. Afterwards I check that every bolt has been tightened (a paint mark across nut and bolt helps), that the right length of thread shows through the nut, that the washers are in place and the parts are fully in contact. I record the torque used.
markingPoints: Bolt grade as specified, with a nut of the matching grade
Hole size as the drawing gives; holes lined up, drilled together where possible
Washers spread the load and protect the surface
Criss-cross tightening, then a torque wrench to the specified figure; lubrication changes the tension
Checks every bolt (paint marks, thread showing, contact) and records the torque

essays.stem: Compare welding, bolting and riveting for joining the parts of a fabricated assembly. Give an advantage and a disadvantage of each, and an example of when you would choose each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Welding joins parts into one piece. It is strong and rigid, seals the joint and needs no holes, but it brings heat and distortion, needs skilled welders and inspection, and cannot be taken apart. I would weld a gate frame or the side frames of a tank stand. Bolting joins parts with bolts, nuts and washers. It can be taken apart and suits site work, as no welding is needed on site, but it needs accurate holes, the bolts can work loose, and the holes weaken the parts a little. I would bolt a stand's cross-bracing to its side frames so that it can be carried to site in pieces, or bolt a bracket to a wall. Riveting joins sheet or thin parts, often with blind rivets put in from one side. It is quick, needs no heat, and can join metals that are hard to weld or are coated, such as galvanised or aluminium sheet, but it is weaker than welding for heavy loads, the rivets are hard to remove and can loosen with vibration. I would rivet a sheet cover or panel to a frame.
markingPoints: Welding: an advantage, a disadvantage and a suitable example
Bolting: an advantage, a disadvantage and a suitable example
Riveting: an advantage, a disadvantage and a suitable example
Choices explained by need (site work, taking apart, coatings, loads)

essays.stem: On final inspection, a frame you built is 5 mm out of square and slightly twisted. Explain how you would find out why, how you would correct it, and how you would record it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the measurements again, to be sure the readings are right, and record how far out it is: the two diagonals, the size, and how much twist there is, using diagonal strings or straight edges on a flat table. Then I look for the cause. Were the parts cut square and to length? Was the frame set out on a flat table, against stops, and checked before tacking? Was the welding order balanced, or was one side welded fully first? Were the clamps released while it was hot? To correct it, if the frame is only tacked, I break the tacks at the corners, pull it square with a clamp across the long diagonal, and tack it again. If it is fully welded, a small error may be corrected by pulling it with a clamp or by flame straightening, if the supervisor approves; otherwise a joint may have to be cut and welded again. After the correction I check it again. I record the fault, the cause, the correction and the final measurements on the inspection sheet or a non-conformance report, and change the method so that it does not happen again.
markingPoints: Re-measures and records the diagonals, size and twist
Finds the cause: cut parts, setting out, weld order, early release
Corrects it: break tacks and pull square, or approved straightening or re-welding
Checks again after the correction
Records it (inspection sheet or NCR) and changes the method

essays.stem: Explain how you would install a fabricated steel gate on site so that it is plumb, level and swings correctly, including the checks you would make.
essays.modelAnswer: Before going to site I check the opening sizes and the drawing, and that the gate, hinges, posts, fixings and tools are ready. On site I mark out the post positions from the opening and check the ground or wall. If the posts are set in concrete, I set them plumb in both directions with a spirit level, at the right spacing and height, brace them, and let the concrete cure for the time given before the gate is hung. If the gate is fixed to a wall, I use anchors that suit the wall and follow the maker's instructions. I fit the hinges with their pins exactly in line, one above the other; if they are not, the gate will swing open or shut on its own. I hang the gate on packers to give the right ground clearance and even gaps, then check that it is level and plumb, swings freely, latches and locks. I check the gaps on each side, tighten all the fixings, and touch up any damaged paint or galvanising. Finally I show the customer how it works and record the checks.
markingPoints: Checks sizes, drawing and kit before going; measures the site
Posts set plumb, spaced, braced and cured (or wall anchors to the maker's instructions)
Hinge pins in line, one above the other
Hangs on packers; checks clearance, level, plumb, swing and latch
Fixings tight, coating touched up, customer shown, checks recorded

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can make sure a team of four works safely and to quality while assembling a large frame. Include the briefing, the roles, lifting and checks.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work I read the drawing and plan the job, then brief the team: what we are building, the order of work, the hazards (heavy parts, hot work, grinding and pinch points) and how each is controlled, and the quality checks. I give each person a clear role, such as setting out, fitting, tacking and welding, inspecting, or leading the lifts, and make sure they are trained for it. I check that PPE is worn and that the tools, clamps and hoist are in good order. I plan each lift: the weight, the lifting gear or the number of people, the route, and one person giving the signals; nobody stands under a load. During the job I watch the work, check the fit-up and tacks at the hold points before welding, and stop any unsafe act or poor work straight away, explaining why. I encourage the team to tell me about problems. At the end I check the finished frame against the drawing, make sure the area is cleaned and tools are put away, and record the checks, any faults and any near misses.
markingPoints: Briefing on the job, sequence, hazards and controls, and quality checks
Clear roles for trained people; PPE and equipment checked
Every lift planned, one person signalling, nobody under the load
Supervises at hold points and stops unsafe acts or poor work
Final check, clean-up, and records of checks, faults and near misses

essays.stem: Describe what should be in a handover pack for a fabricated assembly delivered to a customer, and why each item matters.
essays.modelAnswer: A handover pack is the set of documents that goes to the customer with the finished assembly. It should include the final drawing, marked with any approved changes, so the customer knows exactly what was built. It includes the inspection records: the dimensional checks with the actual measurements, the weld inspection, and the bolt torque record, which show that the work meets the drawing. Any non-conformance reports and concessions are included, so it is clear what was accepted and by whom. The material grade or certificates, and the coating details such as galvanising or the paint system, show what was used and help with future repairs. Fixing and installation instructions, and care and maintenance advice, such as checking bolts and touching up paint, help the customer keep it safe. A delivery note signed by the customer shows that it was received in good order. These records protect both the customer and the Centre if a question or complaint comes up later, and they help if the same item is ordered again.
markingPoints: Final drawing with any approved changes
Inspection records: dimensions, welds and bolt torques
Non-conformance reports or concessions, and material and coating details
Installation, care and maintenance instructions
Signed delivery note, and why the records protect both sides

practical1.title: Building a simple jig and assembling two identical frames, with fit-up hold points and a dimensional report
practical1.brief: Your group will make two identical rectangular frames to the assessor's drawing: about 900 mm × 600 mm in 25 mm square hollow section, each with one centre rail and four corner gussets (tolerance ±2 mm on size and 3 mm on the difference between the diagonals, or as the drawing says). First, as a group, write an assembly plan: the parts list, the order of assembly, where the stops and clamps go, the welding order to control distortion, the hold points, and who does each task. Build a simple jig on the setting-out table, with stops and clamps to hold the parts. Assemble and tack the first frame in the jig. Stop at the fit-up hold point: the inspection leader checks the size, the diagonals, the flatness (with diagonal strings) and the joint gaps, and the assessor signs it off before welding. Weld the frame in the planned order, let it cool, release it and measure it again. Use the jig to make the second frame. Every member fits, tacks or welds at least one joint on each frame and takes part in at least one inspection. Record all measurements before and after welding on the inspection sheet, and write a short report comparing the two frames and the distortion found. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the plan, inspection sheet, report and photos once for the whole group.
materials: Pre-cut 25 mm square hollow section for two frames (eight sides and two centre rails)
Eight corner gussets in 3 mm mild steel plate
Setting-out table, angle or block stops, quick-action clamps and magnetic squares
MMAW or MIG welding set with screens
Tape measure, square, straight edge, string, gap gauge, soapstone and part markers
Angle grinder with a suitable disc
Assembly plan sheet and inspection sheet
photos: The written plan, and the parts checked and marked against the list
The jig built on the table, with stops and clamps
The first frame tacked in the jig
The fit-up hold point: diagonal strings and the tape on the diagonals
The first frame measured after welding and release
Both finished frames side by side
The completed inspection sheet and report
checklist: Helped write the assembly plan and can explain the welding order and the hold points
Checked and marked parts against the parts list
Helped build the jig so that parts locate on stops, with clamps clear of the welds
Fitted and tacked own joints with the right gaps, square and level
Welded own joints in the planned order, with correct PPE and screens
Measured size, diagonals and flatness accurately and recorded them before and after welding
Took part in the report, explaining the distortion found and its likely cause
Moved frames safely with others and left the area clean
safety: Weld only behind screens, with a helmet of the right shade, gloves and flame-resistant clothing
Keep fingers clear as parts are brought together and clamped; clamps and magnets can trap hands
Grind with the guard on, a face shield over safety glasses, and ear protection
Treat all welded parts as hot; mark them and handle them with tongs or gloves
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Assembling a bolted and welded stand from sub-assemblies, with a torque record and a handover pack
practical2.brief: Your group will assemble a small steel stand to the assessor's drawing, for example a model water tank stand about 600 mm square and 800 mm high: two welded side frames as sub-assemblies, joined by bolted cross-braces with M10 grade 8.8 bolts, matching nuts and washers, and a base plate on each leg. First, as a group, plan the sub-assemblies, the order of work, the hold points, the lifting and the roles, and choose one member to lead the briefing. Fit, tack, check and weld the two side frames (each member works on at least one), then check that they match. Mark out, centre punch and drill the bolt holes, clamping mating parts together and drilling them as a pair where possible. Stand the side frames up safely, fit the braces with all bolts finger-tight, and check the stand for square (diagonals), plumb and level. Then tighten the bolts in a criss-cross order with a torque wrench to the figure the assessor gives, and paint-mark each bolt. Every member tightens and records at least two bolts. Make a handover pack: the drawing, the inspection sheet with the actual measurements, the torque record and a short care note for the customer. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Pre-cut 40 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm angle (or 25 mm square hollow section) for the legs and rails
40 mm × 6 mm flat bar for the braces, and four base plates about 100 mm × 100 mm × 6 mm
M10 grade 8.8 bolts with matching nuts and washers
Pedestal drill, drills, centre punch and machine vice or clamps
MMAW or MIG welding set with screens; setting-out table, clamps and magnetic squares
Torque wrench, spanners and a paint marker
Tape measure, square, spirit level and straight edge
Plan sheet, inspection sheet, torque record sheet and a handover pack template
photos: The team briefing, with the plan
The side frames tacked and checked on the table
Holes being drilled with the parts clamped together
The stand assembled finger-tight, being checked for square and plumb
Bolts being tightened in order with the torque wrench
checklist: Took part in the plan and briefing, and knew their role and the hazards
Fitted, tacked or welded at least one joint of a side frame correctly, with correct PPE
Marked out, centre punched and drilled holes accurately, with the work clamped
Lifted and stood the frames up safely with others, using the agreed signals
Checked square, plumb and level, and recorded the readings
Tightened own bolts in the right order to the given torque and paint-marked them
Helped put together the handover pack and can explain what each document is for
safety: Clamp work for drilling and never hold it by hand; tie back loose clothing and hair
Weld behind screens with correct PPE; treat welded parts as hot
Plan every lift, share heavy parts, keep fingers out of pinch points and never stand under a load
Use spanners of the right size; pull rather than push, and keep your balance
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
